overview: ZIP codes are set by the U.S. Postal Service, and some communities share a ZIP code with a neighboring town, which can cause confusion over addresses, taxes, and emergency services. This bill, the CIPZIP Act, requires the Postal Service within 180 days to create a public process for state, local, and tribal governments to request a new ZIP code or a change to existing ZIP code boundaries. The Postal Service would judge requests on their effect on mail service, their cost, and possible future address changes, would give a written reason for any denial, and would offer a contact person and a one-time appeal. Governments denied in the past 10 years could reapply. A seven-year pilot program would let governments offer to pay the Postal Service's costs, and if cost is the only reason for a denial and the government covers it, the Postal Service must approve the change. As of September 14, 2026, it had been approved by a Senate committee and placed on the Senate calendar.
for: Supporters say communities that want their own ZIP code currently face an unclear process, and this gives them a fair hearing, clear reasons, and a way to cover costs themselves.
against: Critics say a flood of new requests could take Postal Service time and money at a moment when it is under financial strain, and frequent ZIP code changes can disrupt mail delivery and address systems.
